questions.stem: A patient survives a large myocardial infarction. Six weeks later, what will most likely occupy the infarcted area?
questions.explanation: Cardiac myocytes are essentially permanent cells; major loss heals by collagen scar. A: Regeneration is insufficient. B: Gliosis is the CNS response. C: Myocytes don't undergo hyperplasia. E: A granuloma is a macrophage aggregate.

questions.stem: Which growth factor is the major mediator of fibrosis, increasing collagen synthesis while reducing ECM degradation?
questions.explanation: TGF-β is the major mediator of fibrosis: it activates fibroblasts and increases collagen/ECM synthesis while reducing ECM degradation. A: VEGF drives angiogenesis. B: PDGF drives fibroblast migration and proliferation but isn't the main fibrogenic mediator. C: HGF drives hepatocyte proliferation. D: FGF-2 drives fibroblast proliferation and angiogenesis.

questions.stem: A clean surgical incision is sutured. About 3 days later, which finding is expected?

options.E: Regenerated hair follicles in the scar

questions.explanation: By ~day 3 macrophages replace neutrophils and granulation tissue begins to fill the incision. B: Neutrophils dominate in the first 24 h, and epithelium bridges by 24–48 h. C: A mature scar takes ~1 month. D: ~80% strength takes ~3 months. E: Appendages aren't restored in a scar.

questions.stem: A patient on long-term high-dose prednisone has an abdominal wound that separates on postoperative day 7. Which mechanism most contributed?
questions.explanation: Glucocorticoids impair healing by suppressing inflammation and collagen synthesis → weak wound → dehiscence. A: Excess TGF-β causes fibrosis. B: A keloid is excess scar. D: More TIMP activity would favor matrix accumulation. E: Contraction isn't the cause of dehiscence.

questions.stem: Which tissue is composed of stable (quiescent) cells that can re-enter the cell cycle after injury?
questions.explanation: Renal tubular cells are stable: normally in G0, they divide after injury (repair also needs preserved tubular basement membranes). A, C, E: Labile, continuously renewing tissues. D: Mature skeletal muscle fibers don't divide; limited regeneration comes from satellite cells.
questions.source: Tissue Repair, notes p2; tutorial s18

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman has a raised, firm scar on her earlobe one year after piercing. Which finding would identify it as a keloid rather than a hypertrophic scar?

options.A: It extends beyond the original wound
options.B: It is raised above the skin surface
options.C: It formed in a wound under tension
options.E: Granulation tissue rises above the surface

questions.explanation: A keloid extends beyond the original wound boundaries and tends to persist or recur; a hypertrophic scar stays within the wound and may regress. B: Both are raised. C: Tension isn't what defines a keloid. D: Both contain excess collagen. E: That is exuberant granulation tissue, which blocks re-epithelialization.
questions.source: Tissue Repair, notes p8; tutorial s27

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with poor diet has gum bleeding, perifollicular hemorrhages, and a surgical wound that won't heal. Which step of collagen synthesis is impaired?
questions.explanation: Scurvy: vitamin C is needed for hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues, so collagen is weak (bleeding gums, poor wound healing). A: Glycosylation doesn't depend on vitamin C. B: Cleavage of procollagen peptides isn't vitamin C–dependent. C: Lysyl oxidase cross-linking needs copper, not vitamin C (outside slides). E: Glycine repeats are set by the amino-acid sequence, not by vitamin C.

questions.stem: A large open leg wound left after debridement heals by second intention. Compared with a sutured surgical incision, which feature is much more prominent?
questions.explanation: Second intention: larger defect, more inflammation and granulation tissue, a larger scar, and much greater contraction by myofibroblasts (α-smooth muscle actin). A: A thin epidermis isn't a defining feature. B: Appendages aren't restored in a scar. D: Re-epithelialization covers a larger area and takes longer. E: More granulation tissue is needed.
questions.source: Tissue Repair, notes p8; tutorial s7

questions.stem: A patient with chronic hepatitis C develops cirrhosis with fibrous septa and regenerative nodules. Which cells are a major source of the collagen in the septa?
questions.explanation: In chronic liver disease, activated hepatic stellate cells are a major source of collagen. A: Hepatocytes form the regenerative nodules, not the septa. B: Macrophages release profibrotic mediators such as TGF-β but don't mainly deposit collagen. C: Endothelial cells form new vessels. D: Lymphocytes release mediators but don't deposit collagen.
questions.source: Tissue Repair, notes p6; tutorial s22
